lesson.title: Before Darwin: How Ideas About Life on Earth Changed
lesson.summary: Long before Charles Darwin, naturalists slowly accumulated evidence that species were not fixed and unchanging, laying the groundwork for the theory of natural selection.
lesson.body:
For a long time, many Western naturalists assumed that species were fixed and unchanging, created once and remaining the same forever after. This idea fit comfortably with religious tradition and with an older philosophical picture of nature as an ordered, static scale of living things. The eighteenth century naturalist Carl Linnaeus developed the system of naming and classifying organisms into nested groups, such as species and genus, that biologists still use today, but Linnaeus himself largely assumed the species he was cataloging were permanent and unchanging.

Fossils began to complicate this picture. Around the turn of the nineteenth century, the naturalist Georges Cuvier studied fossils of animals that no longer existed anywhere on Earth and demonstrated convincingly that extinction was real, entire kinds of organisms had lived and then completely disappeared. That was hard to reconcile with a world of permanently fixed, never changing life. Cuvier still resisted the idea that one species could transform into another, however, and instead explained the pattern in the fossil record through catastrophism, the idea that a series of sudden catastrophes had repeatedly wiped out and then replaced groups of species.

Jean Baptiste Lamarck, in the early 1800s, was among the first naturalists to propose clearly that species do change over time and can give rise to new species, an idea known as transmutation. His proposed mechanism, that traits an organism strengthened or acquired during its own lifetime could be passed on to its offspring, turned out to be incorrect. But the broader claim that species are not fixed, that life has a history of change, was an important conceptual step that later thinkers built on.

The geologist Charles Lyell, in his influential book Principles of Geology, published beginning in 1830, argued for uniformitarianism, the idea that the same slow, gradual processes visible today, such as erosion and sediment deposition, have shaped the Earth's surface over an immense span of time, far longer than a literal reading of a few thousand years would allow. Lyell's deep time gave later naturalists the one thing a theory of gradual biological change absolutely required, enough time for small changes to accumulate into large ones. By the time a young naturalist named Charles Darwin set sail on HMS Beagle in 1831, the ideas that species were not fixed and that the Earth was extraordinarily old were already circulating. What was still missing was a convincing mechanism for how change actually happened, and that is where Darwin's own observations pick up the story.
